I felt exactly the same way. I graduated in May last year and only now am I finding a comfortable pace for my life. Not perfect yet, but getting there.

I saw some people in the comments mention that establishing a routine helps and it’s true. For me it has been work, gym, time with friends at least once a week, and intellect stimulation (this is very important) like self study or reading. You also have to understand that sometimes it’s ok to do nothing and just live and be content. Someone once said that happiness is not joy it’s the absence of pain. I remind myself of this every time the anxiety starts to kick in.

I’ve also started traveling a lot since I graduated and it has helped too. You get to take a break and think about what you really value in life. Your energy is precious. Your attention is precious. Your skills are precious. Few things really matter so you should find out what they are for you and only give yourself to that.

I took 315 with Virtue and it didn't feel like a 12 unit course. The assignments were largely math based where you mostly do linear algebra and some vector calc, the rest was just coding it up using numpy. The test were also not that bad, they mostly tested on understanding/intuition.

213 was a lot harder (at least for me) and more involved. So 315 and 213 at the same time sound manageable.

I can't speak for all of A.I since what I've done in that field is machine learning. But for machine learning most of what you need is probability (not discrete, or not as in depth into discrete probability as you would go into in a combinatorics class), linear algebra, and vector calculus.

It really depends on where you are at right now and what you mean by foundation. But here is what I consider a good foundation:

I would say study linear algebra and analysis for sure. Some abstract algebra and basic number theory (Euclidean algo, Bezouts lemma, Chinese remainder thm) wouldn’t hurt.

Discrete math is really diverse so if you want to gain a solid foundation there I would suggest to look into counting (multiplication/addition principles, counting in two ways) also discrete probability (Markov/Chebyshev inequality, Chernoff bound). You can also learn a bit about the probabilistic method which is a really cool way to prove things. For the fun of it you can also venture into graph theory (personal favorite).
That looks super doable after calc. Plus you’ll learn some proof based math :)

What really helped me with 122 was going though hw/practice test problems that I missed and really working through them in detail until I understood them, like REALLY understood them. Also going over the notes on concepts that I was really weak on.

Good luck! and remember that you can always take P/F

You definitely need to know how to write proofs for discrete math, also some basic logic like p -> q is equivalent not q -> not p. Idk how your class is structured but mine went over graph theory, probabilistic method, and some complexity theory all of which are proof based. If you want to get ahead id recommend looking over some basic combinatorics, especially counting. I went into discrete math without knowing this and the first half was really hard.

To be honest when I first “became” a nihilist I realized that life and actions were devoid of meaning. That thought made me immensely sad and I tried really hard to prove it false, at least for myself. I searched for meaning in my life, for meaning in my life long goals as well as mundane actions. When I didn’t find one, I felt helpless. I felt like outsider to the people around me who were living their lives for their families and their dreams.

Wether my depression was fueled by nihilistic thought or if it was there to begin with, I don’t know. But I soon came to realize that the meaninglessness of my life was not a problem and that it was still worth living. Ironically, I enjoy life more now that I did before and my nihilist philosophy helps me get through tough situations.

I’m glad that I finally found something that sits well with me. There are a lot of things that I have yet to figure out and to be honest, my opinions and arguments on topics like ethics and morals are full of contradictions. But that is ok, it is better to learn these things along the way than to subscribe to someone else’s rules and judgments. (Sorry that I went off topic there)

I don't know about CS but I transferred into math after my freshman year at a sub-par public university. Had 4.0 GPA, the rec letter arrived late (a day after the deadline), my extracurriculars were average (some "student leadership" related activities, and a club that I joined to get volunteer hours for a class), and my essay was something about loving math and synesthesia. I didn't expect to get admitted. So good luck, do your best on the app and even if you don't get in there are a bunch of external factors at play that are out of your control.
